summary.text: A mitochondrion is a double-membrane organelle found in the cells of most eukaryotes, such as animals, plants and fungi.
Mitochondria use aerobic respiration to generate ATP, which is used throughout the cell as a source of chemical energy.
They carry their own genome, similar to bacterial genomes, which led to acceptance of the idea that their ancestors were free-living prokaryotes that fused with eukaryotic cells.

facts.label: Discovered by
facts.value: Albert von Kölliker in 1857, in insect muscles

facts.label: Number per cell
facts.value: None in a mature red blood cell, over 2000 in a liver cell

facts.label: Five compartments
facts.value: Outer membrane, intermembrane space, inner membrane, cristae, matrix

items.prompt: Every part of a cell needs a ready supply of chemical energy. Which organelle makes the ATP that supplies it?

options.label: The nucleus, where most of the DNA is contained
Mitochondria, through aerobic respiration
The cytosol, the fluid around the organelles
The outer nuclear membrane, which holds the genes

items.explain: Mitochondria use aerobic respiration to generate ATP, the cell's source of chemical energy.

items.prompt: Why is a mitochondrion's inner membrane crumpled into ridges instead of lying smooth?

options.label: The extra surface area raises ATP production
It lets large proteins pass through without any signals
It lets the membrane copy the organelle's own genome
It keeps the inner space matching the cytosol

items.explain: The inner membrane is folded to increase surface area, which in turn increases ATP production.

items.prompt: A sugar molecule drifts in the cytosol beside a mitochondrion. How will its concentration in the intermembrane space compare with the cytosol?

options.label: Much lower, since the outer membrane blocks all small molecules
Much higher, since the organelle pulls sugars in using ATP
Zero, since the intermembrane space is sealed off from the cell
About the same, since the outer membrane lets small molecules pass freely

items.explain: The outer membrane is freely permeable to small molecules, so their concentrations in the intermembrane space match the cytosol.

items.prompt: Researchers read the DNA inside a mitochondrion and find it resembles a bacterial genome. What does this suggest about where mitochondria came from?

options.label: They budded off from the nucleus of an early eukaryotic cell
They grew from chloroplasts that lost the ability to photosynthesize
Their ancestors were free-living prokaryotes that fused with eukaryotic cells
They were bacteria that invaded and later replaced the nucleus

items.explain: The bacteria-like genome led to acceptance of symbiogenesis: free-living prokaryotic ancestors permanently fused with eukaryotic cells.

items.prompt: Cell biologists see the outer membrane of a mitochondrion touching the endoplasmic reticulum. What can pass between them there?

options.label: Whole copies of the mitochondrial genome
Lipids, and signals carried by calcium
Finished proteins ready for the nucleus
Sugars that the outer membrane cannot let in

items.explain: Where the outer membrane meets the ER (the MAM), calcium signaling takes place and lipids are transferred.

items.prompt: A toxin tears open the outer membrane of a mitochondrion. What is the serious consequence?

options.label: Proteins leak from the intermembrane space into the cytosol, leading to cell death
The inner membrane quickly loses its folds and stops making ATP
The matrix drains out and the cell divides early
Large proteins from the cytosol flood in and replace the matrix

items.explain: Disruption of the outer membrane lets intermembrane-space proteins leak into the cytosol, leading to cell death.

paragraphs.heading: The cell's power supply
paragraphs.text: Most eukaryotes, including animals, plants and fungi, have organelles called mitochondria in their cells. It has two membranes and uses aerobic respiration to make adenosine triphosphate, or ATP, which the whole cell draws on as a source of chemical energy. Its popular nickname, the powerhouse of the cell, was made widely known by Philip Siekevitz in a 1957 article.

paragraphs.heading: More than energy
paragraphs.text: Mitochondria also take part in signalling, in cells becoming specialised, and in cell death, and they help control the cell cycle and cell growth. They are linked to human conditions such as mitochondrial diseases and heart failure. How many a cell has varies widely: a mature red blood cell has none, while a liver cell can have more than 2000.

paragraphs.heading: Rooms within the organelle
paragraphs.text: In cross section a mitochondrion commonly measures between 0.75 and 3 μm², though size and structure vary a great deal, and it cannot be seen unless stained. It is divided into regions with their own jobs: the outer membrane, the intermembrane space, the inner membrane, the cristae and the matrix. The matrix is the fluid inside the inner membrane. The inner membrane is folded, which gives it more surface area and so raises ATP production.

paragraphs.heading: The outer membrane
paragraphs.text: The outer membrane wraps the whole organelle and is 60 to 75 angstroms thick. It holds many proteins called porins, and a pore-forming protein called VDAC is the main route by which nucleotides, ions and metabolites pass from the cytosol to the intermembrane space and back. Because the outer membrane lets small molecules through freely, the space between the membranes has the same levels of ions and sugars as the cytosol. Larger proteins get in only when a signal at one end binds a translocase, a big protein complex that actively moves them across.

paragraphs.heading: The inner membrane
paragraphs.text: The inner membrane is packed with protein, more than three parts protein to one part phospholipid by weight. Its mix of lipids is unusual: it is rich in cardiolipin, a phospholipid that carries four fatty acids instead of two and may help make the membrane impermeable. Unlike the outer membrane, it has no porins and is highly impermeable to all molecules. Almost every ion and molecule needs a special transporter to enter or leave the matrix.

paragraphs.heading: Once a free-living cell
paragraphs.text: Although most of a eukaryotic cell's DNA is in the nucleus, the mitochondrion carries a genome of its own that resembles bacterial genomes. That finding led to wide acceptance of symbiogenesis, also called endosymbiotic theory. The idea is that free-living prokaryotes, the ancestors of today's mitochondria, fused permanently with eukaryotic cells long ago.

paragraphs.heading: Discovery and name
paragraphs.text: Albert von Kölliker discovered mitochondria in 1857, in the voluntary muscles of insects. Carl Benda coined the name in 1898; it means a thread-like granule.
